metadata.summary: Thessalonica was a free city, provincial center, road junction, and harbor on the Thermaic Gulf in Roman Macedonia. Acts 17 narrates a mission involving Paul and Silas, synagogue hearers, Jason, political accusations, and politarchs; First Thessalonians directly addresses the resulting assembly, while the historical placement of Second Thessalonians depends partly on its disputed authorship and date.

The Thessalonian writings combine living-God, resurrection, day-of-the-Lord, trumpet, prophetic, and apocalyptic language with an address to gentiles turning from idols. The city's Roman setting does not cancel the Jewish scriptural world of the mission and letters.

The city stood on the Via Egnatia at the head of the Thermaic Gulf and retained free-city institutions within Roman provincial rule. Pliny names its status; inscriptions attest politarchs; coins, sanctuaries, votives, associations, and later urban and funerary remains document a socially unequal and religiously plural city. These sources do not identify the assembly's building, full demographics, opponents, or every civic procedure narrated in Acts.

Acts places the mission in a synagogue and names Jewish, God-fearing Greek, and prominent female hearers. First Thessalonians suggests substantial gentile participation, but neither source gives a demographic census or warrants collective Jewish blame for the assembly's affliction.
Second century BCE: construction and development of the Via Egnatia strengthens Thessalonica's east-west connections
Late first century BCE: free-city privileges and early imperial civic coinage shape the Augustan setting
Approximately 49-52 CE: conventional horizon for the mission and First Thessalonians
Before the end of the first century CE: IG X,2 1 32 attests politarchs and civic-cult offices
Second century CE: the British Museum politarch block supplies later local attestation
Second through fourth centuries CE: surviving urban-house and funerary material supplies explicitly later comparisons
